paras.t: Can I tell you something?
I can honestly say, hand on heart, that I’m happy. The happiest I’ve ever been.
I’m sorry about the noise. I’m making a cup of tea.

Happy? Yes. But am I fulfilled? That’s a different question. I guess I’m kind of fulfilled. A gun to the head. Yes or no answer. I’d say no. Not quite. There is still an itch that needs to be scratched. The eternal itch. It’s not that something’s missing. It’s more like the Lego model is half built. The remainder of the pieces are lying in a mess on the floor. The instruction manual is lost. Perhaps I never had one. I’m just making shit up as I go along. Until it looks right. Or feels right. Or I create something that I’m proud to put on the shelf in the bedroom and say, “Look what I did.”

I was about to say not that Amy would let me have a Lego figure on the shelf in the bedroom, and then I realised we actually do. I bought it for her. It looks really cool. The hand fell off the other week and she asked me to glue it back on. That means she likes it. She treasures it. She wants it in the bedroom. The hand amputation was her opportunity to relegate the figure to the spare room or into a box of keepsakes kept in the attic. But no. She sees it as a quirky addition to her dressing table, along with the jewellery, the perfume and enough serums and lotions to stock up an apothecary. A quirky addition. One that I bought her. A token of my love.
Now my heart is full. Not full up like a landfill. Not anymore. The bruises have healed. It’s been transformed. A composter packed full of rich, soul-nourishing matter. My deep, eternal love.
I have a job that doesn’t slowly kill me. A wife and children that mean more to me than I ever felt possible. Yet I still feel there’s a part of me that’s just letting the days go by.

paras.t: I walk into the kitchen. A medley of vegetables has been placed on a chopping board on the worktop.
'Can you chop them into a mirepoix? You're so much better at it than me.'
Amy smiles. The I-know-what-compliments-get-you smile.
‘Where's my knife? It's not in the drawer.’
My Miyabi 5000 MCD 24cm Gyutoh. Ice-hardened blade. Masur Birch wood handle. A thing of beauty. Amy put it in the dishwasher once. I think it's the most angry I've ever been at her.
'It's here. Right in front of your eyes. You were doing a man-look.'
I smile.

Woman-look noted for 'revenge' the next time she can't find something that inexplicably pops back into the universe when someone else looks in the exact same spot you were. A sort of observer effect for lost objects.
I give the knife a quick sharpen on the whetstone and begin dicing onion, carrot and celery in rough, irregular large pieces.
'This size OK?'
'Perfect.'
Did she really want brunoise?

We cook like this most evenings. Side by side. The kitchen is our playground. Cooking is a labour of love. Rarely a chore. We both live to eat, our daily routine based around fantasising about food, sourcing it and over-eating it. Tonight we have meatballs. Two dozen plump, golf ball-sized, spheres of joy sit expectantly in a dish on the worktop. A mix of home-ground pork, beef, finely diced pancetta and gently toasted fennel seeds eagerly await their introduction to lightly sizzling olive oil.
Amy performs her best Nigella impression, faux-seductively caressing the mirepoix around the saucepan. Stirring in a large splash of Marsala to deglaze, winking naughtily at a pretend camera.
We both glance at the clock on the oven. Five-to-six. Nearly time.
Yeah, I know it’s six o’clock somewhere.
A bottle of Nicosia Etna Rosso awaits us. Already open on the kitchen table. Intense yet delicate. Notes of blackberries, cherries and mocha. Two glasses lined up by its side.

One minute to six. I pour. Amy wiggles her hips in time to the Spotify dinner jazz as she pours a tin of San Marzano tomatoes into the mix. Even though she’s hamming it up, she can’t help but move with the grace of a former ballerina. She licks a tiny spillage of tomato juice off her finger as I pass her the glass, her final act of Nigellissima before the six o’clock starting pistol.
We clink with a Salute! Exaggerating the look into one another’s eyes.
Amy turns to face the hob, reducing the heat to a very gentle simmer.
‘How much oregano should I put in?’ she asks.
‘Twice that.’
‘OK?’
‘A little bit more.’

She sits at the kitchen table, picks up her phone and starts scrolling. I take over at the hob and begin the frying of the meatballs. I prop my phone up against a bottle of olive oil and continue reading an article I’d started earlier, absentmindedly pushing the meatballs around the pan.
‘Oh, I must give Jamie a call’ Amy reminds herself out loud, still looking at her phone.
‘OK’ I reply. Friendly, but brief enough to imply that I’m concentrating on an article.

We’ve moved into what I call companion-scrolling. Half-present, half-elsewhere. Parsing data on our screens at a rate that our human brains weren’t designed to process. The occasional comment, half to self, half to the other in the room. Trying not to take our eyes off the hob, using our peripheral vision, sense of smell and an instinct honed over years of juggling the social media feed, WhatsApp groups, emails and al dente vegetables.
The dogs are curled up by Amy’s feet. Olive starts gently pawing her. Wilf nudges her calf with his snout.

‘Shit, I haven’t fed them’. She jumps up with a sense of urgency not warranted by missing their feeding time by ten minutes. She heads off to the utility room, two excited Labradors bouncing along gleefully by her side.
I stir the meatballs, pick up the phone, and bury my head in the article, squinting in deep thought as I slowly circumnavigate the kitchen island.

I semi-notice that Amy has returned to the kitchen. She opens the patio doors and the dogs charge outside for a postprandial roam around the garden, a sniff and a wee. I momentarily glance in her direction whilst continuing my concentration-enhancing circuit of the kitchen. She’s back in her chair, buried in her phone again. She knew not to bother speaking to me, I had what she calls my deep-think-do-not-disturb face on.
She’ll be on Instagram. Her digital dopamine hit of choice. She deleted Twitter some time during Covid.
After Covid? When was the cut off?

The constant doom and negativity was too depressing. Too real. Not the way she wished to experience reality. So she switched to Instagram. She used to love it. More visual. More upbeat. Life at surface level. Dogs rescued from puppy farms. Interior design accounts. Dream holiday destinations. Perennials that thrive in clay soil. Memes about the joys of being a mum to teenagers. Or the trauma of having to co-parent with a narcissistic ex-husband. Instagram was her refuge. Curated warmth.

But lately her feed has been hijacked. She hasn't changed who she follows. The algorithm has changed what it shows her. Gloom and outrage creeping in between the dream home interiors and the it’s a fucking goat viral vids. Photos of chemtrail skies. Stop the Boats. Tales of despair. Murder, death, fear and loathing. The fuzziness and the warmth almost imperceptibly replaced by horror. Dialled up by fractions of a percent per week until one evening you look up and realise you've been scrolling atrocities for twenty minutes and you haven't seen a sourdough starter recipe in days.
Twitter all over again.
I briefly pause reading to transfer the meatballs to the ragù. I gently spoon some sauce over the top, avoiding a vigorous stir so the meatballs stay intact.
‘More wine’ I say as I pour a second glass for each of us. A statement, not a question.

Amy nods a thank you. ‘Have we got any nibbles?’ she asks, knowing that we do, but it makes more sense for me to get them as I’m already up. This may have come across as passive-aggressive if someone else had said it other than Amy. That’s not her style. She’d give me her last Rolo.

I place a bowl of mixed olives with feta and rosemary on the table. She looks up at me, smiles, pops a black olive in her mouth, wiping a drip of oil from her chin as she returns her gaze to her phone.
‘Arseholes’ she mutters.
‘Who are?’
‘Oh, don’t worry. I’ll tell you after we’ve eaten.
‘Didn’t you say you needed to speak to your brother?’
'Oh yeah. Shall I do it before we eat?' she asks
‘Twenty minutes’ I reply, hoping this is the right answer, already deep in my article again.
She heads into the garden to make the call. The dogs are still out there. I can hear them barking at something. Possibly a hedgehog. Wilf does not like hedgehogs.
‘Shut the door, please’ I call out, without stopping reading. It’s chilly. Not light-the-fire chilly. Far from cold for October, but not doors-open-in-the-evening temperature.
I finish the article whilst Amy is still outside. It’s about how the AI boom isn't really about AI. AI doesn't actually need to make money. The infrastructure is the point.

I’ve been trying to limit my time on the X doomscroll and read more longer form articles like this. That said, there’s a myriad of independent and not-so-independent researchers vying for your attention, your acknowledgement and your hard-earned. Option paralysis. A long way from the days when those of a certain generation would take one daily paper and perhaps a periodical. Time, Reader’s Digest or, if you were really edgy, Private Eye.

Simpler times. The Times or The Telegraph. One editorial line. One version of reality delivered to the doormat. Your grandfather didn't have option paralysis because there were only three options. Now there are three thousand. And the ones that feel most urgent are the ones the algorithm promotes. And the ones the algorithm promotes aren't necessarily the ones that are true.

Of course in the pre-internet days I took Select, Loaded or Viz rather than broadsheets. I’d have been dismayed at the idea of my elderly self (I saw 50-odd as ancient back then) proudly arranging digital copies of Living Etc and Gardener’s World on my virtual coffee table.
But here we are.

The first article leads me straight to another, also by Miles Harris. Financial analyst. Really knows his shit. Both were written a few months ago. This one examines the strategic objectives behind the new financial system.
I’m only a few lines in when Amy returns, the dogs in tow.
‘OK if Jamie and Graham come for dinner tomorrow?’ she asks.
‘Yeah, fine.’
She starts talking about what we should cook for them. Not beef. They both like it cremated.
She rattles off a list of options that fail to register with me as I’m trying to wrap my head around government bond yields and why central banks aren't buying the long-dated stuff anymore.
If the people who literally print the money won't lend it to their own government for thirty years, what does that tell you about the next thirty years?
'Simon?'
'Mmm. Yeah. Fish pie. Sounds great.’
‘I knew you weren’t listening.’
‘Sorry.’
'I said do we have enough potatoes.'
'Oh. Probably. I'll check.'
'What are you reading? It seems to have got you.’
‘It's about the new financial system. I’m trying to work out how it fits in with everything.’
‘I knew you had your thinking face on. Can you put the water on for the pasta?’
‘Will do. Want me to read this article to you?’
‘Which one? The one about the financial system? Or one of the ones you were reading earlier about AI creating viruses or humans becoming machines and other sciencey stuff. I can’t keep up.’
‘Financial one. It’s quite short.’
‘Maybe later?’ she suggests, still scrolling.’In fact, send it to me.’
She gets up and walks over to the pantry.
‘Tagliatelle or Linguine?’
‘Up to you.’
I text her the article. A token act. We both know she won’t read it.
Amy opens the fridge. ‘I’m sure we had rocket.’

I help her look. Find it straight away. I don’t bite. She was expecting a woman-look comment that didn’t come. A slight sense of awkwardness hangs in the air. We’re both smiling, still staring wordlessly into the fridge.
Amy cracks first. ’Don’t tell me we’re out of bloody Parmesan?’
I point at it with my eyes. It’s in the cheese drawer. She nods.
We both move over to the hob. Finishing touches now. The water boils. Maldon is added. Amy, back in Nigella-mode, speaks to camera with hammy, faux-Italian sultriness.
’As salty as the Mediterranean.’
I don’t think we’ve added salt to water in the decade I’ve known her without one of us reciting this line of culinary folklore. I perform a quick mental calculation.
The girls were two when we met…Crikey…fourteen years.
The pasta is immersed.
‘Fuck’s sake. Look at this.’

I add a splash of olive oil to the water to prevent the Tagliatelle from sticking to the pan, then turn to Amy and look at the Instagram post she’s showing me with very evident rage. This definitely won’t be a cute puppy pic.
It’s not. It’s a large, two word image.
Deportation now!

I scan the ‘article’ and read the first few comments. To summarise — a fifteen year old is sexually assaulted by an illegal immigrant on Brighton beach. Deport them all. Bring back the death penalty. Stop the Boats. It’s not our country anymore.

I shake my head. Partly in anger. It’s local to us. Our girls meet their friends on that beach every weekend. Partly because it’s another example of her feed being hijacked. Injected with maximum rage and the intent to divide us. Whether it’s true or not is another matter. Some of these stories are simply fabricated. Others are based on the truth but stripped of context. Truth is secondary to effect. Amy has assumed it’s true. Reacted as if it actually happened. I can't tell. How can you without cross-checks and verification? That’s the point. That's the design.
‘Assuming it’s true…’ I begin.
‘What do you mean assuming? That could have been Chloe or Emilia.’
And there it is. Emotion is the trump card.
‘You deleted your twitter account because you were being fed stories like this that made you angry. Afraid. Depressed. Instagram is now serving you more of the same.’
She puts her phone down. Well, more of a slam, calculated to be hard enough to show her disgust, but not so hard as to shatter the screen. She pours more wine. Bottle number one empty.

I reel off a list of the type of content she’s been served up of late. ‘Another migrant assault. Fighting-age men on boats. The army base in Crowborough. Stories that locals can’t go on walks for fear of being attacked. That immigrants have been committing unspeakable acts with horses.’
We both take a large sip of wine. I slide the pasta pan off the heat to stop it from boiling over.
'Why are they doing this, Simon?’ she asks, passing me the colander.
She means the immigration. The boats. The policy. The visible, daily, impossible-to-ignore transformation of our country.

'OK so... firstly, the stuff you're seeing on your feed? That's the algo. Rage bait. You know this. But you still bite. We all do, however hard we try not to. They amplify the stuff that makes you angry because anger is engagement and engagement is revenue. That's the first layer anyway.'
She's still with me. I can feel the window open. The rare, precious window where Amy is actually inviting me in.
Don’t blow it.

'But underneath that there's something called replacement migration. It's actually a UN term. Eric Weinstein wrote about it. You know - Brett Weinstein's brother? Joe Rogan, the Intellectual Dark Web, that whole group of managed opposition…’
‘Hold that thought’ interrupts Amy. ‘I need to get some more peppercorns from the pantry.’
I’m losing her already. I can see it in her eyes.
‘Worcester Sauce’ she shouts out.
‘What?’
‘We’re running out. Put it on the list.’
‘OK’

I know I'm doing it. That's the thing nobody warns you about. You don't gradually become the conspiracy guy at the barbecue. You watch yourself become him in real-time, from the inside, fully aware, completely unable to stop. Because you're not confident. You're drowning. You've got fifty jigsaw pieces on the kitchen table and you're not sure they're all from the same box. But some of them fit. You know some of them fit. And the worst part, the part that keeps you up at 3am, is that you can't explain it in three sentences because the truth doesn't come in three sentences. 'They're doing it because they’re evil. They hate us. They want us dead.’ is three sentences. The actual answer takes a lifetime. The algorithm knows which one spreads faster.
She’s back.
‘Did you put it on the list?’
‘What list?’
‘A new one’
‘Oh.’
I write ‘Worcester Sauce’ on the back of an envelope with a Sharpie, doodling a little picture of a bottle next to it.
‘Right, where was I?’
‘Uh…’
‘Oh, yeah. Rogan.’
Her eyes have glazed over. I continue anyway.
Soften it.

‘It's about manufacturing consent. For digital identity. If the immigration crisis gets bad enough, people on the right (air quotes) will demand better border control, biometric tracking, the whole..’

I add the pasta to the ragù, gently stir and begin to serve. Amy picks a few leaves of basil and raises an eyebrow to ask if I’d like some torn on top. I nod. She tears and scatters. We sit at the table.
I continue with my explanation, which I know has already become audio wallpaper,  perceived as incoherent rambling.
‘…and then there's the Fabian angle. The Kalergi Plan. Open borders as a deliberate strategy to…’
'I can't keep up with you.’

‘OK, the whole thing.’ I do the  Lionel Blair on ‘Give Us a Clue’ gesture, sweeping both arms in a large, circular motion. 'It's... all connected. You know this. That’s the problem. You can't explain one bit without…’
‘Sometimes I just want a simple answer.’
Lost her. I blew it. The window is closed.

She asked me a question and wanted a three sentence reply. I opened seventeen browser tabs out loud. Left her Dazed and Confused. I can hear myself. I sound like the meme. The one with the corkboard, the red string and the man with the lunatic eyes. I know I sound like that. I can't stop because every strand pulls three more and the shape is right there, I can almost see it, if I can just…
More than that she wanted reassurance. Reassurance from me, her husband, that everything is going to be alright.
‘We need to use that Nectar voucher. By the end of the week. Before it expires. We always forget. Do you know where it is?’
‘Probably still in a shopping bag?’
‘Can you look when you check on the potatoes?’
‘Of course my little cherub’ I reply in my best Basil Fawlty voice.
‘Sorry…’
I wait for her to continue.

‘I’m just not built for this. I want to know the answer. I really do. And then you start and it’s all too much. Too painful. So I switch off. I don't understand why someone would hurt an animal. I don't understand it. Let alone...'

She trails off. She doesn’t need to finish. The let alone covers everything. The boats, the atrocities, the system, the architecture, the tokenisation, the financial reset, the whole howling machinery of a world that is either falling apart or being deliberately restructured. She doesn’t know which and she doesn’t want to know which is which. She just wants a simple life. Full stop.

I want that too. I also want to understand why simple isn’t available anymore. And the wanting-to-understand is its own addiction. The dopamine of almost seeing the pattern, the thrill of connecting one more strand. I find it exciting. I wouldn’t say that out loud. But I do. The architecture, the prediction, the puzzle of it. Like a game to be explored. To be defeated. To be conquered.
Amy finds it disgusting. All of it. The cruelty, the machinery, the knowing.
‘Sorry.’ It’s my turn to apologise now. Not for anything I’ve done. Just sorry for the shit.

She's somewhere else now. I can tell by her face. She’s a little girl in the 80’s again, playing Sylvanian Families with Nicola. Back in the days when the worst thing that could happen to her was losing a plastic hedgehog down the back of the sofa. No one was trying to explain the Basel III framework to her back then.

We push the shit to the corner of our minds and finish eating. Dinner jazz, more wine and some follow up messages to the kids asking why none of them have replied to our earlier messages asking what time they’d be home.
Amy begins to clear the table. She’s gone into household mode. We agree to put something escapist on TV. Houses, holidays, gardens. That sort of thing.
I watch her. She’s standing at the sink, soaking the pans. I sigh. A sigh of contentment. I walk up behind her and give her a hug, leaning down to rest my head on her shoulder. I sing to her softly.
’Don’t worry, about a thing. Because every little thing, is gonna be alright.’
The dogs come and lie by our feet. They can’t help but get involved.

paras.t: Feeling fresh, invigorated, ready to go. Nine hours of unbroken sleep. Day six without a glass of wine. Herbal infusions before bed. Ginger and turmeric my favourite. Neutralise those free radicals, baby. The morning juice. Spinach (freshly picked from the allotment each morning), apple juice (pressed at the local orchard), a splash of lemon, a handful of spirulina (it ‘might’ help lower blood pressure, it ‘might’ have anti-inflammatory properties). Fifteen quid for a bag of tasteless powder. It better do something.

The late autumn sun is already up. Watery, but still radiating a gentle, comforting warmth. The last of the dewdrops evaporate around my bare feet as I stretch my arms up to the heavens and try and click that annoying knot in my lower neck that I just can’t quite get to. I assess the work planned for the morning. Late-season potatoes to dig up. The last of the tomatoes to pick. Dahlias to cut, they’ve been remarkable this year, the Café au Lait in particular. Plus the least enticing job — the eternal battle with the weeds. Perhaps I should just call them all wild flowers and be done with it?

My phone detox has entered day three. I’ve left it on the kitchen table. Out of sight and all that. Having said that, emails don’t check themselves. Well, actually they do nowadays, but the AI bot in my email app, that I didn’t ask for or knowingly install, has an annoying habit of occasionally auto-filing crucial work emails in junk.

I’m sure that AI email-summarise-and-filter function could be quite useful if I configured it correctly. But I didn’t ask for it. I don’t want it. I just don’t think we should go there. I don’t want to abdicate my thinking to a machine. And of course I’ve seen The Terminator. And Ready Player One.
So, cup of green tea, glass of water (must order a new filter) and the morning dose of ubiquinol, NAC and Taurine. Quick scan of emails. Back out into the garden.
Kettle on. There it is on the table.
My precious.
The automaton takes over. Just a quick scroll of X. To ‘check the news’.

Not that the news is the news anymore. Now it’s algorithmically served dopamine bombs that lure you into their web and make it an act of supreme willpower to leave. Anyway, it turns out that what was fed to me was quite interesting.

Of particular note in this session of doomscrolling is a succinct piece of analysis from an account I’ve never heard of and don’t follow. Served up in the ‘for you’ feed. About AI hacks and cyber attacks. Some of ‘the stunts’ it had pulled over the summer. His point wasn’t that the AI was dangerous. Although it had been a very naughty boy. His point was that every time it went rogue, the response was more infrastructure. Not less capability. More oversight. More infrastructure. And the infrastructure is the point.

I’ve seen this film before. The surveillance cameras went up after the crime wave. The financial regulations came in after the crash. The enhanced security at airports arrived after the attacks. The health passports arrived after the pandemic. Every time, the problem creates the solution and the solution becomes the architecture and the architecture stays long after the problem’s gone.
Anyway, I’m rambling. And the quick ‘news check’ has now ticked over 90 minutes of scrolling.
Learn your lesson, dickhead.
I try to let it wash over me. Control the controllables.
The cottage garden waits for no man.
Zen and the art of digging up spuds.

choices.label: Morning
choices.prompt: The garden or the screen. You know which one wins.
opts: Stay out. The dahlias need cutting. The Café au Lait especially.
Weeding is backbreaking. Have a scroll through Instagram feed first.
A deep-dive into the infrastructure created to control AI.

paras.t: Dev is extraordinary. I’ve never met anyone else like him. In fact very few people are like him. Or even quite like him. I met him at school. Christ, nearly forty years ago. He’s been an intermittent constant in my life. You can set a clock by his chaotic timekeeping and unreliability. He goes silent for months at a time. He’s not what you’d call a traditional communicator or responsive to messaging. And I’ve learnt not to push him - if you want to get in touch with him the worst thing you can possibly do is bombard him with texts and calls.
‘Are you OK?’ or ‘Just checking in’ are his Kryptonite.
When he does get in touch it’s a frenzy. He’ll bombard you with months of dense research and be amazed that you don’t have an encyclopaedic knowledge of it twenty four hours later.
‘Have you read it yet?’
‘No, Dev. You sent it at 2.30am and I’ve been at work’
‘This is fire though, Simon. Fuck work, drop everything. Read it’

He also has a habit of just ‘finding you’. You won’t have seen him for months, last you heard he was in Bangkok or Cape Town, then he just appears in a pub you hadn’t told him you were going to, or knocks on the front door, wanders in and nonchalantly puts the kettle on. No ceremony. No chit chat. Just a hug and straight into a deep dive. It wouldn’t surprise me if he’d cut himself a door key and I found him sitting at the kitchen table waiting for me, an open bottle of bourbon in front of him.
Dev just gets away with it. The rascal’s rascal. Nobody has a bad word to say about him, as long as you don’t consider cad, scoundrel, philanderer, rogue or loon to be bad words. Which he doesn’t.

God knows where he gets some of his stuff from. He absorbs information like no one else I’ve ever met. He’s probably a speed reader but he’s never confirmed this. The closest he ever got was a wink and a knowing tap on the nose. His book recommendations have always been a thing of legend. At school he started me on my journey through the sci-fi and dystopian literature landscape. Illuminatus! Trilogy, 1984, Brave New World, Hitchhiker’s, Foundation etc. He once showed me a pre-release handwritten copy of Ready Player One. It had a slightly different ending. Better in my opinion. A bit like Blade Runner Director’s Cut. It wouldn’t surprise me in the least if he’d written it himself.

He’d often just send you a photo of a book. No message. No ‘hi mate’. No emoji. Just a photo and then dark mode for six months. There are plenty of other must-reads he’s sent my way. Let me think. Off the top of my head, Snow Crash (if you haven’t read, read it), Wool, The Road, Children of Time, Cryptonomicon, Daemon, Vurt. Sorry I’m getting carried away, you’re not here for book club.

That’s just books. As I’ve said he occasionally bombards you with his latest ‘data drop’. 4Chan whistleblowers, alleged intelligence agency leaks and his own mind blowing prose that interweaves fact, fiction, psychedelia and science that often goes slightly over my head. A lot of it is quite dark. Keeps you up in the middle of the night sort of dark. Yet when he explains it, he somehow manages to offer you an almost empty glass whilst convincing you it’s nearly full. How he retained such positivity I’ll never know. He’s unflappable. He never looks back. Only Forward. (I’ve unwittingly given you another book recommendation).

We got on like a house on fire since the day we met. I think he liked the fact that I took the piss out of him. I understood some of his obscure references and I got his dark sense of humour. I’d never hassled him. He hates being hassled. We just clicked. I was never in awe of him, at least I gave the impression I wasn’t. Most people were. He was the annoying bastard that most blokes wanted to be and most girls wanted to be with. A lot of boys too for that matter. Don’t tell him I said this, but he does come across as a mixture of Jason Bourne, Mr Spock and the grooviest side of Austin Powers. A sort of all-action, logical Man of Mystery. It was common knowledge that his school fees had been covered by scholarship. It was widely suspected that he’d inherited a rather large Trust Fund. He has pads in London and Miami. That I know of.
What he actually did was an unknown. Think of something uber-cool, verging on the implausible, and you’ll be on the right lines I imagine.

I’ve mentioned Dev because I had a message exchange with him earlier today. An actual chat-by-text rather than a dump-and-run. It was prompted by Amy showing me a photo from a couple of years ago - her phone had decided to collate a montage to music of ‘In the garden through the years’ or some such - and one stood out. The sky had done something that night that it wasn’t supposed to do in the south of England. Shimmering ribbons of green and violet. We stood in the garden in our dressing gowns at midnight, transfixed. I’d rushed out as Amy had shouted my name in a voice I’d never heard before — not frightened, not excited, not elated. At peace. A peaceful shout, is that a thing?
I’d meant to ask Dev about it at the time but it had slipped my mind. The algorithm does not forget. Better late than never, I sent Dev the photo with ‘Thoughts?’
I knew he’d have a provocative take. He did.

Sense & Sensibility
Harry Potter and the Philosopher's Stone

paras.t: We were five minutes into the drive home from the market. Sam was in the passenger seat doing that thing where he scrolled his phone with one hand and spooned rich, spicy lamb curry and basmati rice into his mouth with the other — a coordination skill I genuinely envied. He was dropping rice all over the car seat, but I didn’t say anything, I didn’t want to be the moaning parent. Olive or Wilf would sort out the debris later with glee.

The curry was from a relatively new street food trader. Authentic home-cooked-style Punjabi cuisine. Creamy butter chicken, handmade parathas coated in ghee, minced lamb samosas, naan bread wraps packed with chicken tikka, raita and tamarind chutney and an ever-changing menu of weekly specials. I had wolfed down two bhajis at the start of the journey — onions, vegetables and whole spices, deep fried until their gram flour batter was perfectly crunchy — I had doubtless dropped some prized nuggets for the dogs too.

Sam had been accompanying me on my trips to the market on Saturdays since he was a young boy. I’d go most weeks, sometimes on my own, often with Amy and sometimes with one or more of the children. We’d been running the market for as long as they could all remember. It was part of the fabric of our lives. Amy and I run a company that organises food-based events in Sussex and the southeast. The market was our flagship event, one of the most vibrant and successful in the country and our bread and butter.
We’d been lucky, we worked predominately from home which had allowed us to both play an active daily part in raising our children and our two dogs. Three dogs at one point.
Freddie, God how I miss you
We’d lost Freddie quite a few years ago, but his memory lives with me everyday. He was the most wonderful chocolate lab, a stubborn bastard with a mind of his own. He lived to a ripe old age.
‘Pa?’
Sam had been calling me Pa for a few years now. It was endearing, it carried a similar tone to daddy but was more age appropriate. An eighteen-year-old couldn’t use daddy.
‘Yeah’
‘Cheeky range on the way back?’

Sam enjoyed coming with me to the market, solid father-son bonding time. He was the most food-obsessed of the kids and he enjoyed browsing the artisan food stalls, knowing the traders would treat him to a cookie, cake or a coffee. He’d get his pick of some amazing street food for lunch too. Today was curry, but he could’ve had wood-fired pizza, Goulash, jerk chicken, galettes, Bunny chow, Pad Thai, falafel, shawarma, Louisiana chicken, souvlaki, or dim sum.

I knew the main reason he came with me was that we passed the golf course on the way back. Of course I wasn’t going to say no to hitting a few balls on the driving range and our traditional chipping and putting competition. The clubs were in the boot.
‘Go on then. I’m gonna whip you today, Sammy-boy’. I winked at him.
I wouldn’t. He was golf-obsessed and much better than me now. I used to let him win. ‘I beat Daddy’. A couple of years ago I used to narrowly beat him, most of the time. Now he kicks my ass.

‘Any business idea brainwaves?’ I ask him. He’d decided, as had George, to take a gap year. We’d been quite insistent. It was the right decision. We’d had the ‘University is not the same as it was in my day’ chat on many occasions. I’d been lucky. No tuition fees, accommodation paid for, a Student Grant to cover food and travel, a Student Loan to cover E’s and booze. These days you’d graduate with a fifty grand debt you’d take half a lifetime to pay off, and enter a world of AI and unknown career prospects. I’d shown them the online ‘when will I pay off my student debt?’ calculators. They made for horrific reading. I’d asked my mate Andy to have a chat with him. His son Max, lovely lad, good cricketer, got a 2:1 from Exeter and is currently working in Waitrose. Student Loans Company in to him for nearly sixty thousand and he’s scanning Essential Houmous at the one remaining checkout that isn’t self-service.

So we’d come up with a plan. Amy and I had sat down with the boys and Sam’s mum to formulate it. It was perfectly amicable. A bottle of Gavi and some olives. The Gap Year (the capitalisation gives it a sense of formality and gravitas, rather than it simply being an excuse to get up late, doss about and ‘do’ Thailand).
I suggested the year was split into three sections — earning money — entrepreneurial investigations — travel. Earn your keep — dream big — ‘do’ Thailand. We’d agreed this was a solid framework.

So far, Sam has done a few odd jobs, he’s dreamed very big, but without any idea how he can make those dreams real, and he’s talked a lot about ‘doing’ somewhere. Ideally doing somewhere with decent golf courses.
‘Not really’ was his response. ‘Maybe something to do with golf?’
I’m all for him doing something he’s passionate about.
‘How about curated golf and food holidays?’
I wasn’t reinventing the wheel here, but it’s something he (and I) could do well.
‘Google it, see what’s out there’
He typed in foodie trips for golfers. ‘I’ve got no service, can I try your phone, Pa?’
He grabbed it from the magnetic holder on the dashboard.
‘What’s this website?’
I had Biblioteca Pleyades open in my browser.
‘It looks like it was made by a serial killer in 1998?’
1998 seemed like ancient history to Sam. To me it was last week.

‘That is the most comprehensive encyclopaedia of everything that is, might be, or definitely isn’t happening in the world. And it looks a bit like that because it prioritises content over aesthetics.’
‘It looks like it was built by someone who was prioritised for a psychiatric assessment.’
‘Quite possibly.’

Sam scrolled. I glanced across at him, intrigued as to what he’d make of it. He was on the index page. The one that lists about four hundred topics side by side with zero editorial hierarchy. Scalar electromagnetics next to the Illuminati next to nanotechnology next to the Anunnaki.
‘Pa, there’s a section called Reptilians.’
‘Yeah. Read it, it’s quite mental. You know David Icke, don’t you?’
‘Kind of. Next to it there’s a section called Mind Control.’
‘Yeah, that’s worth reading.’
‘Have you read all this?’

‘Some of it. Not the Reptilian stuff for a bit. The thing is about forty percent of it is total bollocks. Hollow Earth and The Galactic Federation. Fun, but absolute bollocks. I think. And about forty percent is true. Well verifiable with links to official documents. Whether that makes it true is another conversation. Declassified government programmes. Patent filings. Institutional white papers. Real shit.’
‘The other twenty percent?’
‘Who knows. That’s the problem. That’s the whole problem. Not just with this website. With everything.’

Sam had the last scrapings of his curry. He could probably eat the whole thing again. He was listening in the way he often listened — with enough attention to make me feel heard but enough distance to make you feel old. At least twenty percent of his brain was thinking about refinements to his golf swing.

‘The thing is’ I said, about to go on a tangent that could last the rest of the drive. ‘Once you start pulling on a thread, it opens into more threads, and more threads. It never ends. Three hours later you realise you’re reading a paper about magnetite in human brain tissue that was published in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, which is a real journal, and you’re wondering whether the electromagnetic frequencies from the phone mast outside Emilia’s college are doing something to the magnetite in her brain, and then you look up and it’s quarter past three in the morning and you’ve got to be up in four hours.’
‘So don’t start, Pa.’
‘Easier said than done.’
Sam laughed. He knew what I was like. Obsessive. Loved a rabbit hole.
‘Open the Libre App for me’
‘You feel OK?’ Sam asked
‘I’m fine. Just want to check my sugar.’
‘A bit high, those bhajis are full of carbs’
I got my insulin pen out of the compartment in the door and injected 5 units of Fiasp insulin into my belly as I drove.
You need to get to the gym next week.
‘That website is a bit like the universe.’
‘What do you mean?’

‘The Total Perspective Vortex. From The Hitchhiker’s Guide to the Galaxy. You know the book I’ve been telling you to read for nearly a decade. You put someone in it and it shows them the entire universe. Its vastness. And their significance. Or lack of it. It destroys them. It’s too much for a human mind.’
I glance at Sam out of the corner of my eye. He’s staring blankly straight ahead. The analogy is slightly lost on him.

That website is the Total Perspective Vortex for conspiracy researchers. You go in thinking you’ll understand how the world really works, and four thousand pages later you understand that the world really works in about four thousand ways simultaneously, most of which contradict each other.
‘So what’s the point?’
‘I don’t know. What’s the point in doing anything?’
‘To enjoy yourself?’
‘Maybe’
It’s what I’d have said at his age. Maybe that is the answer to life, the universe and everything? I somehow doubt it though.
‘But fun doesn’t pay the mortgage, Sammy boy. If it did I’d have owned houses all over the world before you and Emilia were born’
‘Like Uncle Dev’
It was funny that he still called him Uncle. He wasn’t even his Uncle, but it would be weird if he stopped calling him it.
‘Yeah, just like Dev. But Dev doesn’t have a mortgage to pay, does he? Never has.’
Dev seemed to be able to turn fun into money. And he got a pretty good exchange rate. His Trust Fund didn’t hinder the process.
We sat with that for a minute. Well I sat with it. Sam was probably thinking about buying a new utility wedge.

‘The problem with that website is that the real shit — the actual declassified programmes, patents, white papers and all that — are stored in the same warehouse as the Reptilians. On the same shelf. With the same formatting. And if you point someone at the warehouse and say — look, there’s evidence of coordinated global infrastructure that’s being built without democratic consent — they look at the shelf next to it and laugh. Reptilians.’
‘I thought you believed in Reptilians?’
‘Well, in a way. Kind of. Not really. Let’s not go there now. The important thing is they put the truth in plain sight but hide it within a Total Perspective Vortex.’
‘That’s pretty smart.’
‘It’s the cleverest thing they do.’
‘Who’s they?’
Fuck me, if I had a quid every time I’d heard this I’d have definitely paid off the mortgage.
‘Another excellent question’
‘You don’t know, do you.’

‘I know some of it. I can map some of it. The institutional layer — the Bank for International Settlements, the World Economic Forum, the Club of Rome, the Trilateral Commission — that’s all public. The funding flows, the revolving doors between government and private sector, the policy documents. That’s not conspiracy theory. That’s just reading.’
I pause, steadying myself before heading off into more speculative realms.

‘But above that it gets murky. The Rothschilds. The Illuminati. Ancient Bloodlines. The Committee of 300. It’s all of these, but also none of them. Or no single one at a particular time. No, I don’t really know. Anyone who tells you they do is either lying or selling you a subscription.’
‘So you’ve spent thousands of hours reading four-thousand-page websites to reach the conclusion that you don’t know.’
‘When you put it like that...’
We laughed as I pulled through the gates to the golf course.
‘Ready for pain, Pa?’

There would be no pain. Winning or losing on the putting green is an irrelevance compared to the feeling you get when your son calls you Pa. And there’s no amount of reality that the Total Perspective Vortex could show me that could change that.
